title: The one wind in every form
theme: As one wind, entering the world, takes the shape of every form, so the one inner self of all beings takes the shape of every form, and is outside as well.

words.context: Śaṅkara: entering bodies as breath, «प्राणात्मना देहेष्वनुप्रविष्टः»

words.meaning: the inner self of all beings

words.role: predicate; babhūva is understood from the first line
adverb: the self is also outside the forms

samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa (with a karmadhāraya in each member)
samasa.vigraha: सर्वाणि भूतानि सर्वभूतानि, अन्तरः आत्मा अन्तरात्मा, सर्वभूतानाम् अन्तरात्मा
samasa.meaning: the inner self of all beings

morphology.note: A distributive repetition (vīpsā), P. 8.1.4 (नित्यवीप्सयोः), as in 2.2.9: ‘each and every form’.
vāyu, ‘wind’, from √vā, ‘blow’; in the body it is breath (prāṇa), as Śaṅkara’s gloss says.

translation.literal: As wind, one, having entered the world, became corresponding in form to each and every form, so the one inner self of all beings [is] corresponding in form to each and every form, and [is] outside.
translation.readable: As the one wind, entering the world, takes the shape of everything it fills, so the one self within all beings takes the shape of each form, and yet remains outside them.

syntax: The same yathā … tathā comparison as 2.2.9, word for word, with vāyuḥ in place of agniḥ as the subject of the first line.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara calls it simply another illustration, «तथान्यो दृष्टान्तः», and says the rest is the same as before, «रूपं रूपं प्रतिरूपो बभूवेत्यादि समानम्»; Raṅgarāmānuja likewise, «उदाहरणान्तरमाह», and «पूर्ववत्». Neither says what the wind adds to the fire. In Śaṅkara’s gloss the wind enters bodies as breath, so the image moves from things that burn to living bodies.

As in 2.2.9: appearances of the one self (Śaṅkara), the inner ruler in each thing (Raṅgarāmānuja); for Madhva the wind in each thing is the Lord’s counterpart, and conscious souls are his reflections, outside him.

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: Two lines of 22 syllables (11 + 11), as in 2.2.9.

beginner: This verse repeats the one before it almost word for word, with wind in place of fire. The wind is one, yet it fills every space it enters and takes its shape: the inside of a flute, a room, a pair of lungs. So too, Death says, the one self lives inside every being and takes the shape of each body, while also being outside them all. The commentators do not say much more here than ‘another example, the same meaning’. Śaṅkara adds that the wind enters bodies as breath. Repeating a teaching with a second picture is a teacher’s way of helping a hard idea sink in, and the Upaniṣad does it here on purpose. For Madhva, writing just after this verse, the shapes the wind takes are the Lord’s counterparts, and living souls are his reflections, never the Lord himself.
analogy: The same air is the shape of a balloon, a bottle and a breath; it is still one air.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: The image of 2.2.9 again, with wind: as one wind entering the world takes the shape of every form, so does the one inner self of all beings, and it is outside as well.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: «तथान्यो दृष्टान्तः»; the wind enters bodies as breath, «प्राणात्मना देहेष्वनुप्रविष्टः», and the rest is as before, «रूपं रूपं प्रतिरूपो बभूवेत्यादि समानम्». Raṅgarāmānuja: «उदाहरणान्तरमाह», and the meaning is as before, «पूर्ववत्».

commentary.q: Madhva: the wind and the reflections
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: In the source his comment follows the mūla of this mantra (madhva.json files it under 2.2.9): the god Vāyu too is one supporter, there is no other, «एवं देवो वायुरपि धारकोऽन्यो न विद्यते». On the shared second line: Janārdana is one and independent, dwelling within all souls, «एकस्स्वतन्त्रो नान्योऽस्ति सर्वजीवान्तरस्थितः»; the conscious souls in every form are his reflections, «रूपं रूपं प्रति ह्यस्य प्रतिबिम्बाश्च चेतनाः», and they are outside him, never his own nature, «बाह्याश्च ते ततो नास्य स्वरूपं ते कथञ्चन».

advaita.text: A second illustration of the one self appearing many, the wind entering bodies as breath, «प्राणात्मना देहेष्वनुप्रविष्टः»; the meaning is that of 2.2.9.

visistadvaita.text: Another example of the same teaching, «उदाहरणान्तरमाह», read as in 2.2.9: the inner ruler present in each thing.

dvaita.text: Souls are the Lord’s reflections, outside him and never his nature: «बाह्याश्च ते ततो नास्य स्वरूपं ते कथञ्चन».

schools.disagreement: As in 2.2.9: one self appearing as many (Śaṅkara), one inner ruler in each (Raṅgarāmānuja), one independent Lord whose reflections, the souls, remain other than him (Madhva).

parallels.quote: एकस्तथा सर्वभूतान्तरात्मा रूपं रूपं प्रतिरूपो बहिश्च
parallels.note: The preceding mantra, identical except that fire stands where wind stands here.
The inner controller who dwells in all beings.

contemporary.text: Good teachers give a second example when the first has not landed, and the Upaniṣad does the same here. Repetition with variation is how difficult ideas are learned. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: Why might a teacher repeat a lesson with a new example?
reflect.deeper: Fire shows itself by burning, wind by moving and filling. What does each picture let you see about the self that the other does not?
reflect.practice: Notice your breath for a few rounds: the same air, taking the shape of your body as it enters and leaves.

flags.note: As in 2.2.9, the schools differ on what the ‘counterpart forms’ are.

madhva.json has no entry under 2.2.10: Madhva’s comment on this mantra (on wind, and on the souls as his reflections), which in the source follows the mūla of 2.2.10, is filed under 2.2.9 together with his fire verses. It is quoted here from that entry (madhva:2.2.9).
